cells.tense: You're in a stretch where the practice is holding and you're not white-knuckling it.
cells.ask: Take one practice you already keep and do it once today with another person in the room, no talking required. Notice what the practice is like when it isn't kept private.
cells.core:
The time you give your own practice doesn't cut you off from anyone. You can put it down when the day asks for something else and pick it back up without punishing yourself for the gap. The people around you get the ordinary version of you, not the version that's saving itself for the work.

Because that's steady, there's room for the practice to cross into company. You don't have to be good at it in front of anyone, and you don't have to explain it. Doing it with someone nearby, quietly, is a small experiment — it shows you whether the privacy was a choice or a hiding place, and either answer is useful.
cells.sheetLine: Your practice and your people are on the same side right now.
cells.verb: keeping a small practice alive by steady attention rather than by a big push
cells.place: in how you stay in real contact with the people around you

cells.tense: You're living a little ahead of yourself, bracing for the day the practice gives out.
cells.ask: Set a timer for the length you already planned, stop when it rings, and say out loud, 'That's enough for today.' Notice the first minute after you stop.
cells.core:
When this part of you is settled, the practice has a close to it. You do the session, you put the thing down, and you're actually available afterward — to your own evening, to the people in it. The doing and the stopping are both yours.

The stopping is the hard part at the moment. If the practice is finished for the day, something feels unfinished in you, so you keep going back in. Solitude that began as a choice now feels like what the work requires, and ending on time feels like quitting. Pushing harder won't touch that; it's the same loop. Release that comes after something is genuinely complete, not instead of completing it, is the move — and it can only be made today: end the session on purpose, at the mark you set, and let the next hour belong to something else.
cells.sheetLine: You can't finish because finishing feels like failing.

cells.tense: You're still standing at the doorway the last attempt left you at, and it keeps you out of the room.
cells.ask: Do the smallest version of the practice once today — five minutes, where someone can see — then stop, whether you want to keep going or not. Notice how the stopping feels.
cells.core:
There's an ordinary picture of this working: you keep some small thing going, a few minutes most days, and it doesn't have to be good. The people around you don't have to approve of it or even know what it is.

Starting again feels like walking back toward something you'd rather leave where it is, so instead of just not practicing, you've stopped letting it take up room where anyone can see. Effort pushed straight at the practice won't get far — that's the mistake people make here. Giving it the same small slot you'd give any reasonable request from someone else, no more and no less, is what loosens it. The five minutes in view of another person, then stopping, is the act. What you get back is information — whether the being-seen or the stopping is what's being avoided — and that's worth more than another week of not knowing.

cells.tense: The work is already happening — you just haven't said you're the one doing it.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're good at that you didn't set out to learn, then do it once today on purpose, with someone there to see. Notice how it feels to claim it.
cells.core:
When this is integrated, you know which skills are yours. You can say 'I taught myself that' without it being a boast or an apology, and it doesn't need a story about how it just happened. The practice is something you carry into contact with people, not something running in the background while you deny it.

The skill is real and the ownership isn't. You can do the thing and still talk about it like it arrived without you — or like the practice is something you're refusing to have. That's not modesty; it's a missing claim. Moving through the uncertainty without needing the whole picture first is what's called for, and it can happen today: pick one skill you didn't set out to learn, do it on purpose where someone can see, and let the claiming happen in the doing rather than in a decision about whether you're allowed to have it.
cells.sheetLine: The skill is yours. You're still calling it something that happened.
